title: Scale, proportion and visual balance
intro: Proportion relates a piece to its room and neighbouring furniture. Compare alternatives at the same scale while keeping functional access visible.
goals: Review solid, void and visual rhythm

sections.title: Compare alternatives at one scale
sections.text: Draw the room and furniture at a shared scale and retain their original dimensions. Camera perspective can distort perceived size. Use plan to compare footprints and elevation to compare the wall composition. Two differently scaled photographs do not establish a reliable proportional difference.
sections.caption: A shared drawing scale preserves the room-to-piece relationship.

sections.title: Review solid, void and visual rhythm
sections.text: Compare closed areas, open areas and repeated divisions in elevation. Symmetry is one organising approach, not the only form of balance. Connect appearance to construction: moving a divider may change a shelf span and its support needs. Do not approve an elevation separately from its details.
sections.caption: Moving a divider affects both rhythm and shelf construction.

sections.title: Balance proportion with function
sections.text: Compare two alternatives for the same contents and site boundaries. Check capacity, circulation and neighbouring elements for each. If a piece is reduced to improve its appearance, recheck storage and access. State the benefit and trade-off using evidence rather than simply calling one option more attractive.
sections.caption: Keep the functional requirements fixed during comparison.

example.title: Worked case and decision
example.text: A storage elevation has one large closed block beside a door. An alternative distributes the same contents into two blocks with a different surrounding void. Compare scale, door movement and capacity together.
example.decision: Decision: select the option that meets capacity and movement needs while achieving the intended proportions.

quiz.question: What makes a fair comparison?
options: The same scale, contents and site constraints
quiz.explanation: A common reference and brief let you compare the design decision rather than presentation size.

assignment.prompt: Draw two storage elevations for the same contents and justify the solid-and-void arrangement.

faq.question: Is symmetry required for balance?
faq.answer: No. Symmetry is an organising method; an asymmetric arrangement can also balance solids and voids while meeting the brief.
